newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria opens parliamentary election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Algeria opens parliamentary election campaign.

text.p: Campaigning for Algeria's June 5 parliamentary poll, the first since the cancellation of a 1992 election plunged the nation into five years of civil strife, began on Thursday amid new violence.
Elections to the 380-seat National Assembly are seen as a test of whether the government can stop Moslem rebels disrupting the voting and put together a working coalition government.
The task facing the government was underscored by new violence just hours before campaigning began. Moslem rebels slaughtered 30 people at a village south of Algiers, security officials said.
The 16 million voters can chose from 7,747 candidates standing for 39 parties or as independents. Politicians said the new proportional voting system bars a one-party majority win.

Among leading parties trying to win on pledges to restore peace, create jobs and stem corruption are the National Democratic Rally (RND), grouping President Liamine Zeroual supporters, and the Islamist-leaning Movement for a Peaceful Society (MPS).
Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, a candidate for the RND, toured the Algiers Casbah on Thursday -- the first visit by a head of government in five years to the Moslem rebel stronghold, residents said.

Leaders of the Islamist-leaning Movement for a Peaceful Society, seen as the main challenger to the RND to dominate the lower house, began campaigning in Boumerdes, 40 km (25 miles) east of Algiers, by assailing the government over security.
Leading officials in the other 37 parties held similar meetings across Algeria, party officials said.
Diplomats and analysts expect the RND to score well mainly with rural voters who usually support candidates close to government in hope of being rewarded with development projects.
The MPS, whose leader Mahfoud Nahnah won a third of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, has predicted it will win about 40 percent of the vote.

The MPS, Algeria's main legal Islamist party, changed its name to conform to a new law banning parties based on Islam. A second legal Islamist party, Nahda, is also hoping for a large share of the estimated three million Islamist voters.
The main secular party, Socialist Forces Front, will contest the poll after boycotting the presidential election in 1995 and a constitutional referendum last November.
The outlawed Islamic Salvation Front, which had been poised to win the 1992 poll, has called on Algerians to boycott the election, saying it will be neither fair nor free.
Authorities say the poll proves the oil-and-gas-producing nation has come a long way in restoring peace after five years of strife that has claimed about 60,000 lives.

But more than 300 people were killed in attacks during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan early this year. Last month, Moslem rebels killed at least 93 people in a massacre on the closing date for election candidates to register.

According to the constitution adopted last November, the National Assembly and the Council of the Nation (upper house) form the parliament. Two-thirds of the upper house's 144 members will be picked by elected local authorities, while the others will be appointed by the president.
But some diplomats and analysts point out the government has already amended the constitution and tailored an array of laws giving real power to the president.
